metadata.methods_description: Participants read standardized articles while EEG was recorded with a BioSemi ActiveTwo 64-channel system and eye movements were tracked with an SR Research EyeLink 1000 Plus. Mind wandering was annotated at the span level using a retrospective self-report paradigm (ReMind task), and comprehension was assessed with page-level multiple-choice questions.

citation_details.title: Mind-wandering preserves word-level coupling while disrupting comprehension
citation_details.author: Anirudh Natarajan, Paul Sajda
citation_details.abstract: Readers can move their eyes through a page but retain little of its meaning when their minds wander. We tested whether word properties still guide their eyes during these lapses. We analyzed public eye-tracking and electroencephalography (EEG) data from 44 adults who read articles. They marked the text read during each lapse they noticed. We linked these spans to the sentences needed for later comprehension questions. Word frequency, length and surprisal still predicted which words readers skipped and how long they looked at them. Compared with on-task reading, these effects met equivalence bounds of $\pm$10% for skipping and $\pm$20% for gaze duration. Readers spent 14.6% longer on words during lapses. Yet readers answered less accurately when lapses covered sentences needed for a later question. The adjusted difference was 25.7 percentage points for lapses covering all versus none of these sentences. The fixation-related EEG response was 42.7% smaller during lapses. At left posterior-lateral sensor P7, the median increase in alpha power was 10.0%. Occipital sensor Oz showed no reliable increase. These results suggest that word properties can guide the eyes while readers fail to form or retain a useful representation of the text.

citation_details.title: Brain-Language Alignment During Naturalistic Reading and Its Disruption by Mind-Wandering
citation_details.author: Haorui Sun, David C. Jangraw
citation_details.abstract: Encoding models offer a principled framework for linking computational representations of language to neural activity, but most electroencephalography (EEG) evidence for brain--language alignment comes from tightly controlled, word-by-word reading paradigms. Whether such alignment is detectable during naturalistic reading, and how it is affected by lapses in attention, remains unclear. We addressed these questions using ROAMM, a multimodal dataset containing simultaneous EEG and eye-tracking recordings with time-resolved mind-wandering (MW) annotations from 44 participants reading naturalistic texts. Ridge regression encoding models were trained to predict fixation-aligned EEG spectral power and fixation-related potentials (FRPs) from five word-embedding models (GloVe, word2vec, BERT, GPT-2, and Llama 3). Using permutation testing with false discovery rate correction, we found statistically reliable brain--language alignment across both feature types, with contextual embeddings outperforming static embeddings. Spectral alignment was strongest in the alpha and low-beta bands over parietal electrodes, while FRP-based alignment peaked 200--300 ms after fixation onset over central and parietal-occipital regions. Leveraging ROAMM's span-level MW annotations, we further show that brain--language alignment is systematically reduced during MW, an effect that was substantially larger for oscillatory (PSD) than for event-related (FRP) features. These findings demonstrate that modern language-model representations are reflected in EEG activity during naturalistic reading despite the modality's inherent noise, and that fluctuations in attention constitute an underappreciated source of variability in brain--language encoding studies.

citation_details.title: ROAMM: A Benchmark Dataset for Multimodal Human Attention Decoding and EEG-to-Text Modeling During Naturalistic Reading
citation_details.author: David C. Jangraw, Haorui Sun, Ardyn Olszko, Niharika Singh
citation_details.abstract: Note that OSF has a 50 GB storage limit, which prevented us from including all participant data. As a result, we deposited the dataset on OpenNeuro: https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds007629. OpenNeuro requires the dataset to follow the BIDS format standard.
